facts.raw_span: a 4-month history of severe occipital and temporal headaches
headaches that were paroxysmal, aggravated by changes in position
associated with bilateral blurry vision and morning projectile vomiting
a kinetic and static cerebellar syndrome with ataxia, imbalance, uncoordinated movements, bilateral nystagmus, and stage I bilateral papilledema
Routine blood tests were unremarkable
Noncontrast CT of the head showed no abnormalities
an inferior median oval lesion of the cerebellar vermis measuring 40 × 31 × 29 mm
hypointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images
heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration
the lesion filled the foramen of Magendie, exerted mass effect on the medulla
no surrounding edema on FLAIR
elevated choline peak and reduced N-acetyl aspartate signal

concepts.why: The patient's symptoms and imaging findings, including a large cerebellar lesion with heterogeneous enhancement and elevated choline peak, are consistent with medulloblastoma.
The patient's imaging findings, including a cerebellar lesion with heterogeneous enhancement, could be consistent with hemangioblastoma.
The patient's symptoms and imaging findings, including a large cerebellar lesion with heterogeneous enhancement, could be consistent with cerebellar astrocytoma.
The patient's symptoms, including a kinetic and static cerebellar syndrome with ataxia, could be consistent with ataxia telangiectasia.
The patient's symptoms, including a kinetic and static cerebellar syndrome with ataxia, could be consistent with cerebellitis.

rationales.F04: Cerebellar syndrome is more typical of cerebellar tumors like Medulloblastoma, Hemangioblastoma, and Cerebellar Astrocytoma
rationales.F07: Inferior median oval lesion of the cerebellar vermis is suggestive of a cerebellar tumor
rationales.F10: Mass effect on the medulla is more typical of a space-occupying lesion like a tumor
rationales.F12: Elevated choline peak and reduced N-acetyl aspartate signal are suggestive of a tumor

frontier_selector.rationale: The patient's presentation of a 4-month history of severe headaches, cerebellar syndrome, and a large cerebellar vermis lesion with heterogeneous enhancement on MRI is most consistent with a cerebellar tumor, and Medulloblastoma is a common malignant tumor in this location, especially given the patient's age and the tumor's size and imaging characteristics.
